item.research_question: How can high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be designed to simultaneously achieve high fracture strength and high ductility while overcoming issues of inferior castability and compositional segregation?
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); subsequent cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction for some specimens.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (Instron 5569); high-temperature tensile tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (Gleeble 3500); cold rolled specimens tested at room temperature at strain rate 2 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
key_findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.
Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6% (engineering values).
The alloy maintained high strength and ductility up to 700°C, with fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9% at 700°C.
The alloy displayed ultra-high strain hardening with a proof stress of 75 MPa but reaching a fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa.
Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.
The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm³, lower than typical Ni-based superalloys (>8.0 g/cm³).
The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σ_UTS/σ_0.2) was close to 16, far exceeding the 1-3 range of conventional alloys.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations, where alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases (including nanoscale precipitates) pin the movement of dislocations as they pass through the soft phases.
item.limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at the stage of this study.
item.future_work: The authors propose further exploration of new EHEAs based on physical metallurgy principles (atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration) and CALPHAD thermodynamics calculations, as well as further investigations into producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation.
quotes: To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases.
The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a.
Such a high σ UTS /σ 0.2 is also far beyond those of conventional alloys, which are in the range of 1 ~ 3 [27] [28] [29].
